20096-welsh-folk-lore-a-collection-of-th:
Welsh Folk-Lore gathers the folk tales and legends of Wales in one volume. Fairy tales abound in Wales, the book notes at the start. They share much with like tales in other lands, it argues. That likeness points to a common, very old source for them all.

Each tale has a real and an unreal side, the book says. Many forms of one tale show how old and deep its roots run. Readers meet fairies, ghosts, and charms from Welsh oral lore. The book helps keep tales that lived by the fireside, not in print.
20171-gov-bob-taylor-s-tales-the-fiddle-:
Gov. Bob Taylor's Tales gathers stories by Robert Taylor, a famed Tennessee storyteller. Taylor served as governor and won fame for his fiddle and tales. The Fiddle and the Bow and The Paradise of Fools are among them. One tale tells of a great master playing a wondrous violin.

His bow quivered like a bird's wing as he played on. Each quiver held a melody sweeter than human speech, Taylor says. The hearer fell as if into a realm of visions and dreams. Readers get Southern oral tale-telling at its warmest and most musical.
20282-the-working-of-steel-annealing-hea:
The Working of Steel covers annealing, heat treating, and hardening of carbon and alloy steel. Cast iron holds much carbon as graphite, nearly pure carbon itself. That graphite blackens the hands when cast-iron borings are handled at work. Steel turnings, by contrast, do not blacken hands in the same way.

Such fine points guide the smith in heating and dipping steel in water. The book lays out furnaces, colors, tests, and faults in order. Steelworkers and engineers used it as a shop-floor manual daily. Readers get practical metallurgy from the age of rail, ship, and machine.
20472-grace-harlowe-s-plebe-year-at-high:
Grace Harlowe's Plebe Year at High School, published in 1910, opens the Grace Harlowe series. Plebe was slang for a first-year student. Grace enters Oakdale High School and makes the friends who carry the whole series, among them the sunny Nora.

Nora always saw the best in people if there was any best to see. When a classmate dreads her turn to recite, the girls rally round her. The book mixes lessons, games, and scrapes with a steady lesson in loyalty. It set the pattern for dozens of school stories that followed Grace's class.
20763-carpentry-for-boys-in-a-simple-lan:
Making a box opens Carpentry for Boys, a plain guide to first woodwork. Chapters move through beveling, mitering, and first steps in dovetailing. Mortise and tenon joints get their own clear treatment.

Tools, cuts, and joints build up in a set order for young hands. Each task teaches how any wooden structure is put together. Such books once stood in school shops and home sheds across the country. They prize care, true measure, and patience over speed. A boy, or any new learner, could work through these pages and end with real skill in the hands.
20814-the-psychology-of-nations-a-contri:
War, at its simplest, may spring from the herd instinct of early human groups. The Psychology of Nations takes that claim as a starting point. Predatory urges between groups form one plain reading of why wars begin.

From herds, the study moves to crowds, races, and the minds of whole peoples. It seeks laws for how nations feel, think, and act as one. Such crowd studies bloomed in the years around the First World War. This book, a gift to the philosophy of history, shows scholars then straining to grasp mass feeling with new tools.
22075-the-life-of-duty-v-2-a-year-s-plai:
The Life of Duty offers a full year of plain sermons on the Sunday Gospels. Volume II runs from Trinity Sunday to Advent, the second half of the church year. Each sermon takes the Gospel lesson for its Sunday as its text. The preacher's aim, announced in the title, is duty: faith worked out in daily conduct.

Sermons here treat texts like "alive unto God" and "ye shall know them by their fruits." The style is direct, meant for ordinary parish hearers rather than scholars. Sin, service, and self-examination recur week by week. Such Victorian sermon volumes were household reading, and this one shows the plain, practical teaching once heard in English churches.
22375-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-17-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly, volume 17, number 104, appeared in June 1866. The magazine was then a leading American literary monthly. This issue catches the country just after the Civil War ended.

One piece describes parlors in a town called Barton. The two parlors open into each other like no others there. Fine French furnishings fill them, plainer than expected. At the visit described, chairs and tables stand covered for work. Blue yarn, woolen cloth, and cotton lie ready for soldiers' needs. Such scenes show a nation sewing its way back to peace. Readers get period fiction and essays in their original magazine form.
22553-memoirs-of-the-court-of-george-iv-:
Memoirs of the Court of George IV, volume one, covers 1820 to 1830. It draws on original family documents for its court scenes. The queen's case dominates much of this first volume's contents.

Divided opinions respected the queen in the House of Lords. Lord Grenville declared his position in that charged debate there. The Bill of Pains and Penalties was finally abandoned by ministers. The king was left dissatisfied with his ministers' handling of it. Grenville conversed with the king as the affair wound down. Public reaction swung as proceedings against her concluded. Readers get high politics and scandal behind palace doors. George IV's unhappy marriage becomes a national drama in documents.
22656-red-cap-tales-stolen-from-the-trea:
Red Cap Tales retells stories from Sir Walter Scott's Waverley novels for younger readers, as its subtitle jokes: stolen from the treasure chest of the Wizard of the North. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Scott's historical romances, too long and dense for many children, are here shortened and brightened.

The sample finds the narrator at Dryburgh Abbey with a beloved companion. They sit quietly on a rustic bench, gazing toward the aisle where Scott himself lies buried. The pilgrimage mood frames the retellings: to shorten Scott is an act of love, not theft. Tales of Jacobites, border riders, and old Scotland fill the chest. Generations of children met Scott first in such dress, and the book shaped how his stories lived on.
22903-the-expedition-to-borneo-of-h-m-s-:
H.M.S. Dido's expedition to Borneo aimed at suppressing piracy, and its narrative rests on remarkable papers. The writer explains how he drew the story from a man whose career had raised him to high station as a British agent in Borneo. That man shrank from writing his own life, so his rough notes were confided to another's pen.

Behind the modesty stands James Brooke, the White Rajah of Sarawak, whose rise the Dido's cruise supported. The pages mix naval action against pirate fleets with the founding of a personal kingdom. Few imperial stories are stranger than this one. Readers get adventure and statecraft together, told close to the events by men who served in them.
22927-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-18-no-:
Boston's Atlantic Monthly opens its July 1866 number with a strange medical confession. The writer's notes on his own case, he says, were declined by every medical journal he offered them to. The facts were not quite new, editors felt, and the mental conclusions he drew from them were not, in themselves, of medical interest.

That rejected case, a famous account of phantom experience after injury, found its home in fiction's clothing instead. Around it, the issue carries the Atlantic's usual mix of essays, poems, and reviews for a recovering nation. The date matters. America in July 1866 was one year past civil war. A single number like this one shows its best magazine thinking aloud.
a-book-for-all-readers-an-aid-to-the-col: A Book for All Readers, an aid to the collection, use, and preservation of books. The librarian's guide. This book preserves that manual. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
a-critical-examination-of-the-position-o: Thomas Henry Huxley's critical examination of Darwin's work: the Origin weighed and defended. Sharp, fair, and masterly, it settled the science. Darwin's champion at his best. Huxley weighs the Origin and finds it good, the masterly defense.

glinda-of-oz-in-which-are-related-the-ex: The fourteenth and last Oz book Baum finished, featuring the good witch Glinda and Princess Ozma on a mission to stop a war between two peoples. Completed just before Baum's death in 1919, it is a fitting farewell to the land he created. Gentle and good-hearted to the end.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BrownleeWanda_B: On October 29, 1979, a letter went to Dr. Mary S. Metz of Hood College concerning Wanda Brownlee. The letter is attributed, probably, to Harold Weisberg, whose files hold it and whose correspondence ranged across everyone the assassination case touched, academics included. What Weisberg wanted from a Hood College professor about Brownlee sits inside the letter itself. The letter is kept as part of the Weisberg correspondence preserved in the archive.
journal-of-researches-into-the-natural-h:
Charles Darwin's Journal of Researches records his voyage round the world in H.M.S. Beagle. Darwin sailed as naturalist under Captain Fitz Roy. This edition, reprinted in 1913, covers the natural history and geology of every country visited. Darwin dedicates it to Charles Lyell, the geologist whose work shaped his own.

Darwin says plainly that whatever merit his books hold came largely from studying Lyell's writings. The journal itself made his name before the Origin of Species appeared. In it, a young observer describes fossils, islands, volcanoes, and strange living species. His exact, eager notes let readers watch a great scientist forming his questions. The Beagle journal remains a classic of travel and science together.
judith-a-play-in-three-acts-founded-on-t:
Arnold Bennett wrote this play in three acts, first published in London in 1919 and first staged that April at the Devonshire Park Theatre in Eastbourne. Bennett took his plot from the apocryphal Book of Judith. His heroine is the widow Judith of Bethulia, a Hebrew city besieged by the Assyrian army of the general Holofernes, and Lillah McCarthy played the part at the first performance.

The action moves from a street in Bethulia to the valley by the Assyrian camp and into Holofernes' tent, then back to the city on the next day. Elders Ozias, Chabris, and Charmis speak for the trapped city, while Bagoas and Achior serve the Assyrian side. Readers get a tight stage version of the old story, built on talk, dread, and one woman's resolve.
minstrelsy-of-the-scottish-border-volume:
Volume Two of Walter Scott's Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border continues his ballad collection. This third edition is dated 1806. The historical ballads here include Lesley's March and the Battle of Philiphaugh. Others recall the battles of Pentland Hills, Loudonhill, and Bothwell Bridge.

A second part turns from history to romantic ballads. It opens with an ode on Scottish music and an introduction to the Tale of Tamlane. The Young Tamlane and Erlinton follow. Scott prints each ballad with learned notes, preserving songs of covenanting wars and fairy legend side by side. The notes explain each ballad's history and sources.
modern-eloquence-vol-ii-after-dinner-spe:
Thomas B. Reed edited this second volume of Modern Eloquence, a library of speeches and addresses. His associate editors were Justin McCarthy, Rossiter Johnson, and Albert Ellery Bergh. The volume collects after-dinner speeches by speakers whose names run from E to O. A color frontispiece reproduces George W. Maynard's mural Justice from the Library of Congress.

The mural shows Justice holding a globe and an upright naked sword. It belongs to a series of eight panels of the virtues. After-dinner speaking was a serious art in Reed's America, and anthologies like this preserved its models. Reed, a former Speaker of the House, knew oratory from the inside.
mormon-settlement-in-arizona-a-record-of:
James H. McClintock, Arizona's historian, published this record in 1921. His subtitle calls it a record of peaceful conquest of the desert. Chapter One treats Mormon colonization across the West. McClintock credits the pioneers as first farmers in many states, who kept the wilderness broken.

Chapter Two follows the Mormon Battalion of the Mexican War. The battalion marched through the Southwest, took the pueblo of Tucson, and mapped the way through Arizona. Cooke's and Tyler's records, plus soldiers' journals, supply the detail. Chapter Three covers the muster-out and the battalion men who became Arizonans. The book documents irrigation colonies that made desert farming possible.
nasa-tm-19650012562-lunar-landing-dynami:
J Bensko and J L Cortez, in the Physics and Astrophysics Branch at Marshall, wrote this progress report in October 1962. It supports a study of a lunar logistics vehicle, a craft meant to carry supplies to the Moon. Their topic was how much lunar surface models varied, and what that meant for landing.

Nobody yet knew the Moon's surface well. Models of its strength and texture differed widely. Landing gear designed for the wrong surface could fail. Bensko and Cortez set out the range of models then in use. That range told designers how much uncertainty their landing dynamics had to cover.
nasa-tm-19650019799-rotor-stator-interac:
William L Copeland and John L Crigler at Langley presented this noise study in Austin, Texas, in October 1964. Inside an axial-flow compressor, spinning rotor blades pass fixed stator blades. Their interaction makes noise. The team used a single-stage research compressor to study that noise where it spreads into the far field.

Results are given as radiation patterns and frequency spectra. The measured patterns matched calculated results fairly well, the authors report. Compressor noise matters for aircraft that use such machinery. Understanding where the sound goes, and at what pitches, is a first step toward quieter designs for later engines.
nasa-tm-19660024034-supersonic-aerodynam:
Kyle E Wiggins and George E Kaattari present results for a family of triangular wing models at supersonic speeds. Leading edges were swept sixty degrees in the sample's wording, and attack angles ran from slightly negative up to ninety degrees. Speeds covered three settings in the Mach three to Mach five range. The team reports lift, drag, and pitching moment for the family, plus lift-to-drag ratios.

Apex bluntness and cross-section shape were varied to see their effects. A slab model with tip controls and trailing edge flaps also appears. Triangular, or delta, planforms served fighters and entry vehicles alike. Broad test sweeps like this one gave designers a map of the whole family, not just one favored shape.
nasa-tm-19670005590-exposition-of-sundma:
Donald K. Yeomans, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this exposition in December 1966. It explains Sundman's regularization of the three-body problem, the classic puzzle of predicting how three bodies move under their shared gravity. Ordinary equations break down when two bodies collide, and regularization rewrites them so the math stays usable.

Yeomans derives the equations of motion and the integrals of motion in full. He examines a double collision, where two bodies meet while the third stays apart. A new variable removes the singularity at collision, and the distances are expanded as power series in that variable. A second variable removes singularities for any number of such collisions. The series solutions work, he finds, but they converge extremely slowly.
nasa-tm-19680007011-supersonic-aerodynam:
Clyde Hayes, at the Langley Research Center in Virginia, wrote this memorandum in February 1968. Numbered TM X-1491, it reports the supersonic aerodynamic characteristics of a model of an air-to-ground missile. The missile used folding control wings near its midbody, so the model represented both boost and glide configurations.

Wind-tunnel runs at Mach 1.60 and 2.00 varied fin size and sweep angle, plus control wing size and deflection, at two roll angles. The body-fin combination proved generally stable across the tested fin sizes and sweeps. One exception appeared at the higher Mach number and steepest fin sweep, where instability showed at larger angles of attack. Adding the control wings barely changed longitudinal stability but raised normal force and axial force substantially. Deflecting the wings produced useful side and normal forces with almost no pitching or yawing disturbance. The wing fold slots had no aerodynamic effect.
nasa-tm-19680015291-feasibility-of-deter:
C. Prabhakara wrote this May 1968 Goddard Space Flight Center report, numbered X-622-68-203, while linked to the Goddard Institute for Space Studies. He asks whether satellites can measure ozone, the gas high in the air that blocks harmful sunlight, by watching infrared energy leaving Earth. Sharp readings near one ozone band are the key evidence in his test.

Prabhakara builds a method from heat transfer theory and a simple two-part model of how ozone spreads with height. He then checks the method on four case studies and studies its errors with care. His warning is plain: a small error in the measured light grows much larger in the ozone value drawn from it.
nasa-tm-19690003887-hypersonic-aerodynam:
Bernard Spencer Jr. of Langley Research Center tested a logistics spacecraft model at hypersonic speed in this report. The low-fineness-ratio concept used variable geometry for its mission. A fold-down wing stayed stowed during entry, then deployed at subsonic speeds for better low-speed performance.

Tests ran in the Langley 15-inch hypersonic apparatus at Mach 10.03, with the wing retracted. Adding outboard tails raised maximum lift-drag ratio and gave stability across the test range. Two tail sweep options were compared. Varying tail dihedral produced a useful range of trim angles of attack. Elevon deflections widened the trimmable range further. Positive effective dihedral held for all configurations tested, with some reduction at high tail dihedral.
nasa-tm-19700026474-some-effects-of-rada:
Thomas E. Moore prepared this Apollo internal note, number 67-MI-20, for the Manned Spacecraft Center. It studies how the position of the radar antenna affects the lunar module's descent. Radar gives the guidance computer fresh height readings on the way down, and where its antenna sits decides when those readings can begin.

A hybrid simulation compared descent performance for three radar start heights over a realistic lunar terrain model. The study scores each case on fuel-related velocity cost, pitch swings before high gate, and viewing time after it. One clear result: the radar should keep updating altitude steadily from well before high gate. Critical beam angles and zero Doppler conditions are tied back to the simulation outcomes.
nasa-tm-19710008423-design-performance-a:
Henry B. Block, Lawrence A. Mueller, and Fred Boecker Jr. of the Lewis Research Center report here on four large electric heat sources. The heaters were built for liquid-metal systems tied to the SNAP-8 power program. On the ground, they stood in for a nuclear reactor's heat.

Two heaters were compact units that copied the reactor's heat behavior closely. The other two were heavy-duty units built above all for reliability. The first pair was built at one power level, and the second pair at a higher one. The paper covers their design, their performance, and what test runs taught the team.
nasa-tm-19710016878-hypersonic-aerodynam:
Charles L Ladson of the Langley Research Center wrote this April 1970 memorandum, NASA TM X-1994. It reports force tests on the DL-4, a lifting entry vehicle shape. Such winged shapes glide back through the atmosphere instead of falling like a capsule. The test shape had a lift to drag ratio near three, strong for a reentry craft.

Ladson gathered data at Mach 6 and Mach 10 in air, and Mach 20 in helium. He compared the readings with theory to find where the math held and where it failed. Separate Mach 10 runs tried tip fin and body changes. The goal was a shape stable around all three axes during entry.
nasa-tm-19710018639-effects-of-retrorock:
Edwin E Davenport and Edwin E Lee Jr of the Langley Research Center studied how retrorocket exhaust changes the drag of a blunt cone. The shape was a one hundred twenty degree cone, like the aeroshell of a planetary entry craft. Braking rockets firing forward into the airflow could disturb that flow. The team tested the idea in the Langley sixteen foot transonic tunnel.

Blunted cones carried simulated retrothrust nozzles with four, eight, or twelve jets. Runs held the cone at zero angle of attack and low subsonic speeds. The results showed a strong interaction between the exhaust and the drag. Once heat shield needs were met, dropping the front cone face would help.
observations-on-the-effects-of-the-corn-:
Thomas Robert Malthus wrote this short work on trade in grain. It was printed in London in 1814. Malthus taught political economy at the East India College. He wrote as Parliament prepared to review the Corn Laws. Those laws controlled imports of grain into Britain.

Malthus asks how the laws affect farming and national wealth. He also asks what happens when corn prices rise or fall. He argues that earlier debate missed key points on both sides. He answers Adam Smith on the bounty for exporting corn. The work offers a clear case in an old policy fight. He writes in a calm, reasoned style for lawmakers.
ohio-biological-survey-bull-10-vol-11-no:
Bruce Fink wrote part four of The Ascomycetes of Ohio. Leafy Corrington wrote part five in the same bulletin. Ohio State University published the bulletin in 1921. Part four treats the lichen family called Lecideaceae. Part five treats the family called Peltigeraceae.

Fink explains how lichens fit among other ascomycete fungi. He notes close links to related lichen families. He uses the language of modern systematic mycology. The papers classify species and describe their structures. They served working botanists who identify Ohio lichens in the field. Careful keys and notes support that field work throughout.
on-the-art-of-writing-lectures-delivered:
Arthur Quiller-Couch delivered these lectures at Cambridge in 1913 and 1914. Cambridge University Press first published them in 1916. Quiller-Couch held the King Edward chair of English there. He was also a fellow of Jesus College. The book opens with his inaugural lecture.

The lectures teach students how to write clear English. Quiller-Couch stresses plain words, order, and honest thought. He warns against jargon and empty, showy phrases. His spoken style keeps the lectures lively and direct. Generations of students learned style from this book. It remains a classic manual for young writers.
podcast-joerogan-WDqWc_ucs-o:
Neuroscientist Amishi Jha joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1723 to talk about attention. Jha studies how the mind focuses and wanders, and she has tested mindfulness training on soldiers, students, and surgeons. Her subject is the one resource every listener feels slipping.

She explains her finding that attention works like a flashlight, strong but easy to knock off target, and that short daily practice can steady it. Rogan asks how phones and stress wear the beam down. The episode turns lab science into a usable skill, with a researcher who speaks in clear, kind terms.
robinson-fewer-and-better-babies-birth-c: Fewer and better babies, birth control, or The limitations of offspring, by Robinson. The eugenic pamphlet. This book preserves that work. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
the-life-of-columbus-from-his-own-letter: Edward Everett Hale's life of Columbus built from the admiral's own letters and journals, letting the discoverer tell his tale in his own words. Storms, mutinies, and the wonder of new lands come straight from the source. History with the salt spray still on it, Victorian style.
washington-and-his-comrades-in-arms-a-ch: George Wrong's chronicle of Washington and his comrades: the Revolution's leaders. Clear and inspiring, it tells the founding story. A fine popular history. Wrong's Washington leads the founding generation, the Revolution clearly told, a fine popular history.
